::: {#def-gaussian-univariate}
#### Univariate Gaussian Distribution

The univariate Gaussian distribution with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$:

$$ \mathcal{N}(x | \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} $$
:::

::::

The factor
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}$ ensures the distribution integrates to 1.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Heights are the textbook example of an approximately Gaussian quantity. The example uses the rule that about $68\%$ of the mass
lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

::: {#exm-msf-gaussian-heights}
#### Human heights

For example, if human heights follow $\mathcal{N}(170,
100)$ (mean 170cm, standard deviation 10cm), approximately 68% of people have heights between 160cm and 180cm (within one standard
deviation of the mean).
:::
::::

Probabilities for any Gaussian reduce to the standard normal by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. The
exercise uses this for a tail probability and evaluates the peak of the density.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader standardises a height threshold and reads a tail probability of the standard normal. The second part evaluates the
density at its maximum.

::: {#exr-msf-gaussian-tail}
#### Tall people

For heights $\sim \mathcal{N}(170, 100)$, estimate $\mathbb{P}(\text{height} > 190)$, and find the maximum value of the density.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(190 - 170)/10 = 2$, so the probability is $\mathbb{P}(Z > 2) \approx 0.0228$ for a standard normal $Z$. The density is largest at
$x = \mu$, where it equals $1/\sqrt{2\pi \cdot 100} = 1/(10\sqrt{2\pi}) \approx 0.0399$ per cm.
:::
::::

For multivariate data, such as feature vectors $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, we use the multivariate Gaussian:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gaussian-multivariate}
#### Multivariate Gaussian Distribution

The multivariate Gaussian distribution with mean vector $\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$:

$$ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} | \boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d |\Sigma|}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})} $$
:::

::::

The covariance matrix must be positive
semidefinite (see [Linear Algebra Recap](../appendices-and-technical-background/index.qmd#sec-linear-algebra-recap)). The Gaussian distribution is central to linear regression ([Linear Models](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/supervised-learning/index.qmd#sec-linear-models)),
Gaussian processes, and many other machine learning models [@deisenroth2020mml, Sec. 6.5, p. 197; @bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 3.2, p. 70].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
With zero mean and identity covariance the formula becomes a product of univariate standard normals. The example writes this
out in two dimensions.

::: {#exm-msf-gaussian-standard-2d}
#### The standard bivariate Gaussian

For $d = 2$, $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\Sigma = \mathbf{I}$: $|\Sigma| = 1$ and
$\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}) = \frac{1}{2\pi} e^{-\|\mathbf{x}\|^2/2} = \mathcal{N}(x_1|0, 1)\,
\mathcal{N}(x_2|0, 1)$. Its contours are circles centred at the origin.
:::
::::

The factorisation persists whenever the covariance is diagonal, which means the coordinates are independent. The exercise asks
for the proof in two dimensions.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader computes the determinant and inverse of a diagonal covariance and inserts them into the formula. The exponent splits
into a sum, so the density splits into a product.

::: {#exr-msf-gaussian-diagonal}
#### Diagonal covariance

Show that for $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2)$, $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} | \boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma) =
\mathcal{N}(x_1 | \mu_1, \sigma_1^2)\,\mathcal{N}(x_2 | \mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\Sigma| = \sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2$, so $\sqrt{(2\pi)^2|\Sigma|} = \sqrt{2\pi\sigma_1^2}\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_2^2}$. Also
$\Sigma^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(1/\sigma_1^2, 1/\sigma_2^2)$, so $(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x} -
\boldsymbol{\mu}) = (x_1 - \mu_1)^2/\sigma_1^2 + (x_2 - \mu_2)^2/\sigma_2^2$, and the exponential of the sum is the product of the
exponentials. Grouping the factors gives the two univariate densities.
:::
::::

### Multinomial Distribution

The multinomial distribution generalizes the binomial to cases with more than two outcomes. Consider rolling a six-sided die $n$
times: the counts of each face follow a multinomial distribution. If we roll the die 60 times, the expected count for each face is
10, but the actual counts will vary according to:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-multinomial}
#### Multinomial Distribution

The multinomial distribution for counts $(x_1, \ldots, x_k)$ of $k$ outcomes in $n$ trials with probabilities $(p_1, \ldots, p_k)$:

$$ \operatorname{Mult}(x_1, \ldots, x_k | n, p_1, \ldots, p_k) = \frac{n!}{x_1! \cdots x_k!} p_1^{x_1} \cdots p_k^{x_k} $$

where $\sum_{i=1}^k x_i = n$ and $\sum_{i=1}^k p_i = 1$.
:::

::::

This distribution is fundamental in
text classification and topic modeling, where we model word counts in documents.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A small number of rolls keeps the factorials manageable. The example asks for three different faces in three rolls.

::: {#exm-msf-multinomial-three-rolls}
#### Three rolls, three faces

The probability that three rolls of a fair die show the faces $1$, $2$ and $3$ once each, in any order, is
$\operatorname{Mult}(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0 | 3, \tfrac{1}{6}, \dots, \tfrac{1}{6}) = \frac{3!}{1!\,1!\,1!}\left(\tfrac{1}{6}\right)^3 =
\frac{6}{216} = \frac{1}{36}$.
:::
::::

The multinomial should contain the binomial as its two-outcome case. The exercise asks the reader to confirm this.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader sets $k = 2$ and eliminates the second count and probability with the constraints. The binomial formula appears.

::: {#exr-msf-multinomial-binomial}
#### Two outcomes

Show that for $k = 2$ the multinomial distribution reduces to the binomial distribution of @def-binomial.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x_2 = n - x_1$ and $p_2 = 1 - p_1$, $\operatorname{Mult}(x_1, x_2 | n, p_1, p_2) = \frac{n!}{x_1!(n - x_1)!}p_1^{x_1}(1 -
p_1)^{n - x_1} = \operatorname{Bin}(x_1 | n, p_1)$.
:::
::::

## Stochastic Processes and Markov Decision Processes {#sec-msf-stochastic-processes}

Sequential decision problems need random variables that evolve in time. This section defines stochastic processes, the Markov
property that makes them tractable, and the Markov decision processes on which reinforcement learning is built. For more on this topic, see @zhao2025rl [Sec. 1.7, p. 11; App. A, p. 237] and @aggarwalProbabilityStatisticsMachine2024 [Sec. 10.2].

### Stochastic Processes

Single random variables describe one measurement; many problems involve a whole sequence of them. A stochastic process is such a
sequence.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-stochastic-process}
#### Stochastic Process

A stochastic process is a collection of random variables indexed by time, representing the evolution of a system with inherent
randomness.
:::

::::

For example, the daily closing price of a stock, the position of a robot navigating a room, or the state of a game
being played all constitute stochastic processes. Understanding these processes is crucial for sequential decision-making
problems, which form the foundation of reinforcement learning ([Reinforcement Learning](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/reinforcement-learning/index.qmd#sec-reinforcement-learning)).

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two simplest processes are an independent sequence and a sum of independent steps. Both are built from the coin and die
experiments of the previous sections.

::: {#exm-msf-stochastic-process-walk}
#### Repeated rolls and a random walk

Repeated rolls of a die give a process $X_1, X_2, \dots$ of independent, identically distributed random variables. Adding
independent steps $\xi_t = \pm 1$, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, gives the simple random walk $S_0 = 0$,
$S_t = S_{t-1} + \xi_t$, whose values at different times are dependent.
:::
::::

The distribution of a random walk spreads out over time. The exercise computes it after two steps.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader lists the four equally likely step sequences of length two. The PMF, mean and variance of $S_2$ follow.

::: {#exr-msf-random-walk-two-steps}
#### Two steps of a random walk

For the simple random walk of @exm-msf-stochastic-process-walk, find the PMF, mean and variance of $S_2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The step pairs $(+1, +1)$, $(+1, -1)$, $(-1, +1)$, $(-1, -1)$ each have probability $\frac{1}{4}$, so $\mathbb{P}(S_2 = 2) = \frac{1}{4}$,
$\mathbb{P}(S_2 = 0) = \frac{1}{2}$, $\mathbb{P}(S_2 = -2) = \frac{1}{4}$. Then $\mathbb{E}[S_2] = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S_2) = \mathbb{E}[S_2^2] =
\frac{1}{4} \cdot 4 + \frac{1}{4} \cdot 4 = 2$.
:::
::::

### Markov Property

Many stochastic processes satisfy a special property that greatly simplifies their analysis: the future depends only on the
present, not on the past. This is called the Markov property or "memorylessness." Formally, for a sequence of states $S_0, S_1,
S_2, \ldots$:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-markov-property}
#### Markov Property

$$ \mathbb{P}(S_{t+1} | S_t, S_{t-1}, \ldots, S_0) = \mathbb{P}(S_{t+1} | S_t) $$
:::

::::

The property is easiest to appreciate through one process that has it and one that does not. The examples give both.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A board game is Markov as long as the state records the full board. The first example explains why the history of moves is
irrelevant.

::: {#exm-msf-markov-chess}
#### Chess

To understand this intuitively, consider a chess game. If we know the current board position (the present state), we can determine
all legal moves and their consequences without knowing how the game reached this position. The history of moves doesn't
matter—only the current configuration. This property dramatically reduces the complexity of modeling sequential processes.
:::

Weather is the usual counterexample, because yesterday's weather carries information that today's does not. The second example
shows how the property can fail, and why it is still used as an approximation.

::: {#exm-msf-markov-weather}
#### Weather

As a counterexample, consider predicting tomorrow's weather. If we only know today's weather (sunny), our prediction might be less
accurate than if we also knew yesterday's weather (rainy). In this case, the Markov property might not hold perfectly, though it
often serves as a useful approximation.
:::
::::

A process built by adding independent increments forgets everything except its current value. The exercise asks the reader to
prove this for the random walk.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader writes $S_{t+1}$ in terms of $S_t$ and a fresh step. Independence of the step from the past gives the Markov
property.

::: {#exr-msf-markov-random-walk}
#### The random walk is Markov

Show that the simple random walk of @exm-msf-stochastic-process-walk has the Markov property.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$S_{t+1} = S_t + \xi_{t+1}$, and $\xi_{t+1}$ is independent of $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_t$, hence of $S_0, \dots, S_t$. So
$\mathbb{P}(S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s, S_{t-1}, \ldots, S_0) = \mathbb{P}(\xi_{t+1} = s' - s)$, which depends only on $s$; this equals
$\mathbb{P}(S_{t+1} = s' | S_t = s)$.
:::
::::

### Markov Decision Processes

A Markov Decision Process (MDP) extends the Markov property to include decision-making. An MDP models situations where an agent
interacts with an environment: the agent observes the current state, chooses an action, receives a reward, and transitions to a
new state. This framework is fundamental to reinforcement learning ([Reinforcement Learning Foundations](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/reinforcement-learning/index.qmd#sec-rl-foundations)).

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-mdp}
#### Markov Decision Process (MDP)

A Markov Decision Process (MDP) is a tuple $(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma)$ where:

- $\mathcal{S}$ is the state space, the set of all possible states the system can be in. For a robot navigating a grid, this might
be all possible positions.

- $\mathcal{A}$ is the action space, the set of all possible actions. For the robot, this might be {move north, south, east,
  west}.

- $P(s' | s, a)$ is the state transition probability function, giving the probability of reaching state $s'$ when taking action
  $a$ in state $s$. For example, if the robot tries to move north, it might succeed with probability 0.9 but slip and move east with
  probability 0.1 due to wheel slippage.

- $R(s, a, s')$ is the reward function, specifying the immediate reward received after transitioning from state $s$ to state $s'$
  via action $a$. The robot might receive +10 for reaching a goal location, -1 for each step (to encourage efficiency), and -100 for
  hitting an obstacle.

- $\gamma \in [0, 1]$ is the discount factor, which determines how much the agent values future rewards compared to immediate
  ones. With $\gamma = 0$, the agent is myopic and only cares about immediate rewards. With $\gamma$ close to 1, the agent is
  far-sighted and values future rewards almost as much as immediate ones.
:::

::::

The objective in an MDP is to find a policy $\pi: \mathcal{S} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}$, a mapping from states to actions, that
maximizes the expected cumulative discounted reward:

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t R(S_t, A_t, S_{t+1})\right] $$

This framework provides the mathematical foundation for reinforcement learning algorithms discussed in [Reinforcement Learning](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/reinforcement-learning/index.qmd#sec-reinforcement-learning)
[@zhao2025rl, Secs. 1.6-1.7, pp. 9-11].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest useful MDP has two states and two actions. The example computes the discounted return of one policy by summing a
geometric series.

::: {#exm-msf-mdp-two-states}
#### Two states, stay or switch

Let $\mathcal{S} = \{s_1, s_2\}$, $\mathcal{A} = \{\text{stay}, \text{switch}\}$ with deterministic transitions,
$R(s, a, s') = 1$ if $s' = s_2$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\gamma = 0.9$. The policy "switch in $s_1$, stay in $s_2$" earns $1$ at
every step from $s_2$, a return of $\sum_t 0.9^t = 10$, and from $s_1$ it earns $1 + 0.9 \cdot 10 = 10$ as well.
:::
::::

The discount factor decides how an agent weighs a delayed goal against step costs. The exercise computes returns in a small
corridor for several discount factors.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader sums the discounted rewards along the shortest path to a goal. Changing $\gamma$ changes how much the goal reward
counts.

::: {#exr-msf-mdp-corridor}
#### A corridor with a goal

A robot moves deterministically along cells $1 \to 2 \to 3$; the transition into the goal cell $3$ gives reward $+10$, and the
other step gives $-1$. Find the return of the path from cell $1$ for $\gamma = 1$, $\gamma = 0.9$ and $\gamma = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rewards are $-1$ then $+10$. The return is $-1 + \gamma \cdot 10$: $9$ for $\gamma = 1$, $8$ for $\gamma = 0.9$, and $-1$ for
$\gamma = 0$, where the myopic agent sees only the immediate step cost.
:::
::::

## Statistical Concepts {#sec-msf-statistical-concepts}

Statistical concepts provide the tools for summarizing, analyzing, and making inferences from data. These concepts are essential
for understanding how machine learning algorithms learn from finite samples and generalize to new data. For more on this topic, see @zhao2025rl [App. A, pp. 239-241] and @aggarwalProbabilityStatisticsMachine2024 [Sec. 3.9, pp. 97-104].

### Expected Value

The expected value (or expectation) of a random variable represents its long-run average value. Imagine rolling a fair six-sided
die many times: while any single roll is unpredictable, the average value converges to 3.5. This is the expected value.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-expected-value}
#### Expected Value

For a discrete random variable $X$ taking values $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ with probabilities $p(x_i)$:

$$ \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_i x_i p(x_i) $$

For a continuous random variable with probability density function $p(x)$:

$$ \mathbb{E}[X] = \int x p(x) dx $$
:::

::::

The discrete formula is a weighted average of the values, the weights being their probabilities. The example confirms the value
$3.5$ for the die.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Each face has weight $\frac{1}{6}$, so the expectation is the plain average of the faces. This is the long-run average quoted
above.

::: {#exm-msf-expected-value-die}
#### The fair die

For example, if $X$ represents the outcome of rolling a die, $\mathbb{E}[X] = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + \cdots +
6 \cdot \frac{1}{6} = 3.5$.
:::
::::

The continuous formula replaces the sum by an integral against the density. The exercise uses both formulas once.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader computes one continuous and one discrete expectation. Both are needed later in the chapter.

::: {#exr-msf-expected-value-uniform}
#### Two expectations

Compute $\mathbb{E}[X]$ for $X$ uniform on $[0, 1]$ (density $p(x) = 1$) and for $X \sim \operatorname{Bern}(p)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int_0^1 x \, dx = \frac{1}{2}$, and $0 \cdot (1 - p) + 1 \cdot p = p$.
:::
::::

The expectation is linear: $\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y]$ for any constants $a, b$ and random variables
$X, Y$. This property is fundamental in analyzing learning algorithms, where we often need to compute expected losses or errors.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-msf-linearity-expectation}
#### Linearity of Expectation

For any constants $a, b$ and random variables $X, Y$ with finite expectations,
$\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y]$.
:::

::::

Proof (discrete case): by @def-expected-value applied to the pair, $\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = \sum_{x, y}(ax + by)\,p_{X,Y}(x, y) =
a\sum_x x \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x, y) + b\sum_y y \sum_x p_{X,Y}(x, y)$, and @prp-msf-total-probability turns the inner sums into
$p_X(x)$ and $p_Y(y)$. The continuous case is the same with integrals. No independence is needed.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Linearity gives the expected sum of two dice without listing the 36 outcomes. The two dice need not even be independent.

::: {#exm-msf-linearity-two-dice}
#### Sum of two dice

If $X_1, X_2$ are two die rolls, $\mathbb{E}[X_1 + X_2] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7$.
:::
::::

Writing a count as a sum of indicators is the main trick that linearity enables. The exercise uses it for the binomial mean.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader expresses a binomial count as a sum of Bernoulli variables. The second part is a direct evaluation on the die.

::: {#exr-msf-linearity-binomial}
#### The binomial mean by linearity

(a) Show that $k \sim \operatorname{Bin}(n, p)$ has mean $np$. (b) Compute $\mathbb{E}[X - 2Y]$ on the die.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $k = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ with $X_i \sim \operatorname{Bern}(p)$, so $\mathbb{E}[k] = \sum_i \mathbb{E}[X_i] = np$. (b)
$\mathbb{E}[X] - 2\mathbb{E}[Y] = 3.5 - 2 \cdot 0.5 = 2.5$.
:::
::::

### Variance and Covariance

While the expected value tells us the center of a distribution, the variance measures its spread. A distribution with high
variance has values that are typically far from the mean, while low variance indicates values cluster tightly around the mean.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-variance}
#### Variance

The variance is defined as the expected squared deviation from the mean:

$$ \operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 $$
:::

::::

The second equality provides a computational shortcut: we can compute the variance from the expectation of $X^2$ and the square of
the expectation of $X$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The shortcut formula needs only $\mathbb{E}[X^2]$ and $\mathbb{E}[X]$. The example applies it to the die.

::: {#exm-msf-variance-die}
#### Variance of the die

For our die example, $\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 1^2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 2^2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + \cdots + 6^2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} = 15.17$,
so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = 15.17 - 3.5^2 = 2.92$. The standard deviation $\sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)} \approx 1.71$ provides a measure
of spread in the same units as $X$.
:::
::::

Rescaling a random variable rescales its spread, while shifting it does not. The exercise proves this rule and applies it.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader uses linearity of expectation inside the definition of variance. The result is then applied to the die.

::: {#exr-msf-variance-affine}
#### Variance of an affine transformation

Show that $\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and compute $\operatorname{Var}(2X + 1)$ for the die.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b$, so $aX + b - \mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a(X - \mathbb{E}[X])$, and squaring and taking
expectations gives $a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$. For the die, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{35}{12}$, so $\operatorname{Var}(2X + 1) = \frac{35}{3} \approx
11.67$.
:::
::::

Variance describes one variable; to see how two variables move together, one replaces the square by a product of deviations.
The result is the covariance.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-covariance}
#### Covariance

The covariance measures how two random variables vary together. If $X$ and $Y$ tend to be large together and small together, their
covariance is positive. If one tends to be large when the other is small, the covariance is negative. If they vary independently,
the covariance is zero (though zero covariance doesn't guarantee independence).

$$ \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])] = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] $$
:::

::::

The sign of the covariance carries most of its meaning. The examples give one qualitative case and one exact computation on the
die.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Height and weight are the standard case of positive covariance. No numbers are needed to see the sign.

::: {#exm-msf-covariance-height-weight}
#### Height and weight

For example, consider height $X$ and weight $Y$ in humans. These variables have positive covariance because taller people tend to
weigh more.
:::

On the die, the face value and the parity indicator are positively related, because even faces are on average larger. The second
example computes the covariance exactly.

::: {#exm-msf-covariance-die}
#### Face and parity

For the die example, $\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)=\sum_{x,y} p_{X, Y}(x, y) xy - \mathbb{E}[X] \mathbb{E}[Y] = 0.25$.
:::
::::

The parenthetical remark in the definition, that zero covariance does not imply independence, deserves a concrete
counterexample. The exercise provides one and also relates covariance to variance.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader first checks that a variable's covariance with itself is its variance. Then a symmetric example shows uncorrelated but
dependent variables.

::: {#exr-msf-covariance-uncorrelated}
#### Uncorrelated but dependent

(a) Show that $\operatorname{Cov}(X, X) = \operatorname{Var}(X)$. (b) Let $X$ be uniform on $\{-1, 0, 1\}$ and $Y = X^2$. Show that
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) = 0$ but $X$ and $Y$ are not independent.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) Set $Y = X$ in the definition. (b) $\mathbb{E}[X] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X^3] = 0$, so the covariance is $0$.
But $p_{X,Y}(0, 1) = 0$ while $p_X(0)p_Y(1) = \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{2}{3} \neq 0$.
:::
::::

Collecting the covariances of all pairs of coordinates of a random vector gives a matrix. This matrix is the covariance matrix.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-covariance-matrix}
#### Covariance Matrix

The covariance matrix $\Sigma$ for a random vector $\mathbf{x} = [X_1, \ldots, X_d]^\top$ has entries $\Sigma_{ij} =
\operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j)$. In matrix form, the covariance matrix of $\mathbf{x}$ is

$$\Sigma=\mathbb{E} \left[(\mathbf{x}- \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}])(\mathbf{x}-\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}])^\top\right] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$$
:::

::::

This matrix appears in the multivariate Gaussian distribution and is central to dimensionality reduction
techniques like PCA ([Dimensionality Reduction](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/unsupervised-learning/index.qmd#sec-dimensionality-reduction)).

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The three variables of the die give a $3 \times 3$ covariance matrix. Its diagonal holds the variances and its off-diagonal
entries the covariances.

::: {#exm-msf-covariance-matrix-die}
#### The die vector $(X, Y, Z)$

The covariance
matrix of the random vector $(X, Y, Z)$ is

$$\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \operatorname{Var}(X) & \operatorname{Cov}(X, Y) & \operatorname{Cov}(X, Z) \\ \operatorname{Cov}(Y, X) & \operatorname{Var}(Y) &
\operatorname{Cov}(Y, Z) \\ \operatorname{Cov}(Z, X) & \operatorname{Cov}(Z, Y) & \operatorname{Var}(Z) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2.92 & 0.25 & -0.75 \\
0.25 & 0.25 & -\frac{1}{12} \\ -0.75 & -\frac{1}{12} & 0.25 \end{pmatrix}$$
:::
::::

Every covariance matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite, which is why the multivariate Gaussian can use it. The exercise
asks for the proof.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader relates the quadratic form $\mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{u}$ to the variance of a scalar random variable. Non-negativity
of variance does the rest.

::: {#exr-msf-covariance-matrix-psd}
#### Covariance matrices are positive semidefinite

Show that $\Sigma$ is symmetric and that $\mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{u} = \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ for every
$\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^d$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = \operatorname{Cov}(X_j, X_i)$ gives symmetry. With $\boldsymbol{\mu} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}]$,
$\mathbf{u}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{u} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{u}^\top(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\mathbf{u}] =
\mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{u}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu})^2] = \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{u}^\top\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$.
:::
::::

### Conditional Expectation

Conditioning on an event changes the distribution, and with it the average. The conditional expectation is the average under the
conditional PMF.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-conditional-expectation}
#### Conditional Expectation

The conditional expectation of $X$ given $Y = y$ is

$$\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y]=\sum_x x p_{X|Y}(x \mid y)$$
:::

::::

Knowing that the face is even shifts the average upward. The example quantifies the shift.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Given an even face, the faces $2, 4, 6$ are equally likely. Their average is the conditional expectation.

::: {#exm-msf-conditional-expectation-die}
#### Average of an even face

For the die, $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=1] = \sum_x x p_{X|Y}(x \mid y=1) = (2 + 4 + 6) \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 4$.
:::
::::

The same computation can be done for the other conditioning events of the running example. The exercise asks for two of them.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader averages the odd faces and the low faces. Both answers are used in the next exercise.

::: {#exr-msf-conditional-expectation-odd-low}
#### Odd and low faces

Compute $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = 0]$, $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Z = 1]$ and $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Z = 0]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbb{E}[X | Y = 0] = (1 + 3 + 5)/3 = 3$, $\mathbb{E}[X | Z = 1] = (1 + 2 + 3)/3 = 2$ and $\mathbb{E}[X | Z = 0] =
(4 + 5 + 6)/3 = 5$.
:::
::::

Averaging the conditional expectations with the right weights must return the overall expectation. The law of total expectation
recovers the expectation from the conditional ones:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-msf-total-expectation}
#### Law of Total Expectation

$$\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_y \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=y] p_Y(y)$$
:::

::::

Proof: $\sum_y \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]\,p_Y(y) = \sum_y \sum_x x\, p_{X|Y}(x \mid y)\,p_Y(y) = \sum_x x \sum_y p_{X,Y}(x, y) =
\sum_x x\, p_X(x)$, by @def-msf-conditional-pmf and @prp-msf-total-probability.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Conditioning on parity splits the die into two halves with averages $4$ and $3$. Weighting each by one half returns $3.5$.

::: {#exm-msf-total-expectation-die}
#### Recovering the mean of the die

For the die, $\mathbb{E}[X]= \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=1] p_Y(1) + \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y=0] p_Y(0) = \frac{4 + 3}{2} = 3.5$.
:::
::::

Any other partition of the die must give the same answer. The exercise checks this with the low-face indicator and applies the law
to a two-stage experiment.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader conditions on $Z$ instead of $Y$ and then on a coin that decides how many dice are rolled. In both cases the law of
total expectation does the bookkeeping.

::: {#exr-msf-total-expectation-two-stage}
#### Conditioning in two ways

(a) Verify the law of total expectation on the die with $Z$ in place of $Y$. (b) A fair coin decides whether one die or two dice
are rolled; find the expected total.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 5 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 3.5$ (@exr-msf-conditional-expectation-odd-low). (b) The conditional
expectations are $3.5$ and $7$ (@exm-msf-linearity-two-dice), so the expected total is $\frac{1}{2}(3.5 + 7) = 5.25$.
:::
::::

### Bias-Variance Decomposition

One of the most important concepts in machine learning is the bias-variance decomposition, which
explains why models fail to generalize. Consider a regression problem where we want to predict $y = f(x) + \varepsilon$, where $f(x)$
is the true function and $\varepsilon$ is irreducible noise with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2$.

Suppose we train a model $\hat{f}(x)$ on a training set. If we could repeat this process with many different training sets drawn
from the same distribution, the expected squared error at a point $x$ decomposes as [@james2023statistical, Sec. 2.2.2, eq. 2.7; @aggarwalProbabilityStatisticsMachine2024, Sec. 6.7, pp. 284-287]:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#thm-msf-bias-variance}
#### Bias-Variance Decomposition

If the noise $\varepsilon$ at $x$ is independent of the training set, then

$$ \mathbb{E}[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2] = \underbrace{(f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)])^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} +
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)])^2]}_{\text{Variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{Irreducible
Error}} $$
:::

::::

Proof: write $m = \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]$, so that $y - \hat{f}(x) = (f(x) - m) + (m - \hat{f}(x)) + \varepsilon$. Squaring gives the
three squares plus three cross terms. The term $f(x) - m$ is a constant, and $\mathbb{E}[m - \hat{f}(x)] = 0$ and
$\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$, so the cross terms with $f(x) - m$ have zero expectation; the cross term
$2\,\mathbb{E}[(m - \hat{f}(x))\varepsilon]$ factorises by independence into $2\,\mathbb{E}[m - \hat{f}(x)]\,\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon] = 0$.
What remains is $(f(x) - m)^2 + \mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(x) - m)^2] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2]$, and $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon^2] = \sigma^2$.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The example reads each of the three terms for a model that is too simple for the data. A linear fit to a quadratic truth has
high bias and low variance.

::: {#exm-msf-bias-variance-linear-fit}
#### A linear model for a quadratic truth

Let's understand each term through an example. Suppose the true relationship is $f(x) = x^2$, but we fit a linear model
$\hat{f}(x) = ax + b$:

The bias $(f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)])^2$ measures how far the average prediction is from the truth. A linear model cannot
capture the quadratic relationship, so it will systematically underpredict or overpredict. This is high bias—the model is too
simple.

- The variance $\mathbb{E}[(\hat{f}(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)])^2]$ measures how much the predictions vary across different
training sets. A linear model has relatively low variance because its predictions don't change dramatically with different
training data.

This is the noise $\sigma^2$ in the data itself, which no model can eliminate.
:::
::::

The two extreme estimators, one that ignores the data and one that averages it, show the trade-off in closed form. The exercise
computes all three terms for both.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader evaluates the decomposition for a constant predictor and for a sample mean. One has zero variance, the other zero
bias.

::: {#exr-msf-bias-variance-sample-mean}
#### A constant and a sample mean

Let $f(x) = \mu$ be constant and the training set be $y_i = \mu + \varepsilon_i$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, with independent noise of
variance $\sigma^2$. Compute bias, variance and expected error for (a) $\hat{f} = c$, a fixed number, and (b)
$\hat{f} = \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}] = c$, so the bias$^2$ is $(\mu - c)^2$, the variance $0$, and the expected error
$(\mu - c)^2 + \sigma^2$. (b) $\mathbb{E}[\bar{y}] = \mu$, so the bias is $0$; $\operatorname{Var}(\bar{y}) = \sigma^2/n$ by independence
and @exr-msf-variance-affine; the expected error at a new point is $\sigma^2/n + \sigma^2$.
:::
::::

Now consider fitting a high-degree polynomial. This flexible model can fit $f(x) = x^2$ well (low bias), but it's sensitive to the
specific training data and might fit the noise (high variance). The bias-variance trade-off is fundamental: simple models have
high bias but low variance, while complex models have low bias but high variance. The goal is to find the sweet spot that
minimizes total error, as discussed in [Foundations of Learning Theory](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/foundations-of-learning-theory/index.qmd#sec-learning-theory) [@james2023statistical, Sec. 2.2.2, pp. 31-33].

## Optimization Foundations {#sec-optimization}

Optimization is the engine that powers machine learning. Nearly every learning algorithm can be framed as an optimization problem:
find the parameters $\mathbf{w}$ that minimize a loss function $L(\mathbf{w})$. For example, in linear regression we minimize the
squared error, in logistic regression we minimize the cross-entropy loss, and in neural networks we minimize task-specific
objectives. Understanding optimization is therefore essential for both implementing and analyzing machine learning algorithms. For more on this topic, see @deisenroth2020mml [Sec. 7.1, pp. 227-232], @bishop2024deeplearning [Secs. 7.2.2-7.2.4, pp. 214-216] and @zhao2025rl [Sec. 6.4.4, pp. 119-120].

### Gradient Descent

Gradient-based optimization is the workhorse of modern machine learning, used to train everything from simple linear models to
massive neural networks with billions of parameters. The fundamental insight is beautifully simple: if we want to minimize a
function, we should move in the direction where it decreases most rapidly. The gradient tells us this direction.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gradient}
#### Gradient

The gradient $\nabla L(\mathbf{w})$ is a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase of the loss function
$L(\mathbf{w})$. To minimize the loss, we move in the opposite direction:

$$ \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \eta \nabla L(\mathbf{w}_t) $$
:::

::::

The learning rate $\eta > 0$ controls the step size. If $\eta$ is too small, we take tiny steps and convergence is painfully
slow—imagine taking millimeter steps down the mountain. If $\eta$ is too large, we might overshoot the minimum and even
diverge—like taking such large steps that we leap past the valley and up the other side.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A one-dimensional quadratic shows all three regimes of the learning rate. The update becomes multiplication by a fixed factor.

::: {#exm-msf-gradient-descent-quadratic}
#### Gradient descent on $w^2$

For example, consider minimizing $L(w) = w^2$. The gradient is $\nabla L(w) = 2w$, so the update rule becomes $w_{t+1} = w_t -
2\eta w_t = (1 - 2\eta)w_t$. Starting from $w_0 = 1$ with $\eta = 0.1$, we get the sequence $1, 0.8, 0.64, 0.512, \ldots$
converging to 0. But with $\eta = 0.6$, we get $1, -0.2, 0.04, -0.008, \ldots$ which oscillates but still converges. With $\eta =
1$, we get $1, -1, 1, -1, \ldots$ which oscillates forever.
:::
::::

In several dimensions, each direction of a quadratic can have its own curvature, and the step size must suit the steepest one.
The exercise shows this on an elongated bowl.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader computes a gradient, takes one step, and finds the range of learning rates for which the iteration converges. The
steeper coordinate sets the limit.

::: {#exr-msf-gradient-descent-anisotropic}
#### An elongated bowl

For $L(w_1, w_2) = w_1^2 + 3w_2^2$, compute $\nabla L$, one gradient step from $(1, 1)$ with $\eta = 0.1$, and the learning
rates for which gradient descent converges from every starting point.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\nabla L = (2w_1, 6w_2)$, so the step gives $(1 - 0.2, 1 - 0.6) = (0.8, 0.4)$. The coordinates evolve as
$w_1 \leftarrow (1 - 2\eta)w_1$ and $w_2 \leftarrow (1 - 6\eta)w_2$; both factors have absolute value below $1$ exactly when
$0 < \eta < 1/3$.
:::
::::

### Stochastic Gradient Descent

In machine learning, the loss function typically has the form $L(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n L_i(\mathbf{w})$, where
$L_i$ is the loss on the $i$-th training example and $n$ might be millions or billions. Computing the full gradient $\nabla
L(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \nabla L_i(\mathbf{w})$ requires processing the entire dataset at each step—prohibitively
expensive for large datasets.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-sgd}
#### Stochastic Gradient Descent

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) approximates the gradient using a single randomly selected example:

$$ \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \eta \nabla L_i(\mathbf{w}_t) $$
:::

::::

This gradient estimate is noisy—sometimes it points in the wrong direction—but it's unbiased: $\mathbb{E}[\nabla L_i(\mathbf{w})]
= \nabla L(\mathbf{w})$. On average, we're moving in the right direction, and we can take many more steps in the time it would
take to compute one full gradient. The noise can even be beneficial, helping the algorithm escape shallow local minima.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Fitting a single number to three data points is small enough to list every possible stochastic gradient. The example takes one
SGD step and checks unbiasedness.

::: {#exm-msf-sgd-three-points}
#### Estimating a mean with SGD

Take $L_i(w) = \frac{1}{2}(w - y_i)^2$ with data $y = (1, 2, 3)$, so $\nabla L_i(w) = w - y_i$ and $\nabla L(w) = w - 2$. At
$w = 0$ with $\eta = 0.5$, drawing $i = 3$ gives $w = 0 - 0.5(0 - 3) = 1.5$. The three possible gradients at $w = 0$ are
$-1, -2, -3$, whose average $-2$ equals $\nabla L(0)$.
:::
::::

Unbiasedness is a one-line computation, while the noise of the estimate is measured by its variance. The exercise asks for
both.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader proves unbiasedness for a uniformly drawn index. The variance is then computed for the data of the example.

::: {#exr-msf-sgd-unbiased}
#### Mean and variance of the stochastic gradient

(a) Show that $\mathbb{E}[\nabla L_i(\mathbf{w})] = \nabla L(\mathbf{w})$ when $i$ is uniform on $\{1, \dots, n\}$. (b) For
@exm-msf-sgd-three-points, find the variance of $\nabla L_i(0)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\mathbb{E}[\nabla L_i(\mathbf{w})] = \sum_i \frac{1}{n}\nabla L_i(\mathbf{w}) = \nabla L(\mathbf{w})$. (b) The values
$-1, -2, -3$ have mean $-2$, so the variance is $\frac{1}{3}(1 + 0 + 1) = \frac{2}{3}$.
:::
::::

Mini-batch Gradient Descent strikes a balance between full-batch gradient descent and SGD. Instead of using one example or all
examples, we use a small random subset (mini-batch) of size $b$ (typically 32, 64, or 256):

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-minibatch-gd}
#### Mini-batch Gradient Descent

Mini-batch gradient descent uses a subset of size $b$:

$$ \mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \eta \frac{1}{b}\sum_{i \in \text{batch}} \nabla L_i(\mathbf{w}_t) $$
:::

::::

Mini-batches reduce the noise in the gradient estimate while remaining computationally efficient. They also enable efficient
parallel computation on modern hardware (GPUs), where processing 64 examples simultaneously is nearly as fast as processing one.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
With the data of @exm-msf-sgd-three-points, a batch of two points averages two stochastic gradients. The example shows one
such batch.

::: {#exm-msf-minibatch-two}
#### A batch of two

At $w = 0$, the batch $\{1, 3\}$ gives $\frac{1}{2}((0 - 1) + (0 - 3)) = -2$, which here happens to equal the full gradient.
The batch $\{1, 2\}$ gives $-1.5$, closer to $-2$ than the worst single-example gradients $-1$ and $-3$.
:::
::::

The noise reduction can be quantified: averaging $b$ independent draws divides the variance by $b$. The exercise asks for this
calculation.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader assumes the batch indices are drawn independently and uniformly, with replacement. The variance of an average of
independent variables does the rest.

::: {#exr-msf-minibatch-variance}
#### Variance of a mini-batch gradient

Show that if the $b$ batch indices are drawn independently and uniformly, the mini-batch gradient has the variance of one
stochastic gradient divided by $b$. Evaluate it for @exm-msf-sgd-three-points with $b = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The batch gradient is $\frac{1}{b}\sum_{j=1}^b G_j$ with $G_j$ independent copies of $\nabla L_i(\mathbf{w})$. Variances of
independent variables add, and @exr-msf-variance-affine gives the factor $1/b^2$, so the variance is $b \cdot v/b^2 = v/b$. With
$v = 2/3$ (@exr-msf-sgd-unbiased) and $b = 2$, it is $1/3$.
:::
::::

### Advanced Optimizers

Standard gradient descent treats all parameters equally and uses a fixed learning rate. Modern optimizers improve on this in
various ways:

Momentum adds a velocity term that accumulates gradients over time, helping the optimizer build up speed in consistent directions
and dampen oscillations. Think of a ball rolling down a hill: it doesn't just respond to the current slope but also has momentum
from previous motion.

RMSProp and Adam adapt the learning rate for each parameter individually based on the history of gradients. Parameters with large,
consistent gradients get smaller learning rates (to avoid overshooting), while parameters with small or inconsistent gradients get
larger learning rates (to make progress). Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) combines momentum with adaptive learning rates and has
become the default optimizer for many deep learning applications.

These advanced optimizers are essential for training deep neural networks ([Neural Networks](../../fundamentals-of-machine-learning/supervised-learning/index.qmd#sec-neural-networks)), where the loss landscape can be
highly non-convex with many saddle points and plateaus [@deisenroth2020mml, Sec. 7.1.2, pp. 230-231; @bishop2024deeplearning, Secs. 7.1, 7.3, pp. 210-224; @shalev2014ml, Sec. 20.5, p. 236; @aggarwalLinearAlgebraOptimization2020, Sec. 5.3, pp. 212-216].

### Stochastic Approximation

Stochastic approximation methods are a class of iterative algorithms used to find the root or optimum of a function that can only
be observed with noise. These methods are fundamental to online learning and are widely used in reinforcement learning for
updating value functions and policies.

The general form of a stochastic approximation algorithm is:

$$ \mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta_k \hat{g}(\mathbf{w}_k) $$

where $\hat{g}(\mathbf{w}_k)$ is a noisy estimate of the gradient of the objective function, and $\{\eta_k\}$ is a sequence of
step sizes. For the algorithm to converge, the step sizes must satisfy the Robbins-Monro conditions:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-robbins-monro}
#### Robbins-Monro Conditions

A sequence of step sizes $\{\eta_k\}$ satisfies the Robbins-Monro conditions if

$$ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \eta_k = \infty \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{k=1}^\infty \eta_k^2 < \infty $$
:::

::::

The first condition ensures that the algorithm can reach any point, while the second condition ensures that the noise in the
gradient estimates eventually cancels out.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) can be viewed as a special case of stochastic approximation. In reinforcement learning,
stochastic approximation is used in algorithms like Temporal-Difference (TD) learning to update value function estimates based on
noisy returns from the environment [@zhao2025rl, Secs. 6.2, 6.4, 7.1, pp. 103-106, 114-115, 126-127; @theodoridis2025ml, Sec. 5.4, pp. 192-194].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The step sizes $\eta_k = 1/k$ are the standard choice that satisfies both conditions. With them, stochastic approximation
computes a running mean.

::: {#exm-msf-robbins-monro-running-mean}
#### The running mean

$\eta_k = 1/k$ satisfies the conditions, since $\sum_k 1/k$ diverges and $\sum_k 1/k^2 = \pi^2/6$. With
$\hat{g}(w_k) = w_k - x_k$ for observations $x_1, x_2, \dots$, the update $w_{k+1} = w_k - \frac{1}{k}(w_k - x_k)$ gives
$w_2 = x_1$, $w_3 = \frac{1}{2}(x_1 + x_2)$ and in general $w_{k+1} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j \le k} x_j$. A constant step violates the
second condition, and $\eta_k = 1/k^2$ violates the first.
:::
::::

Polynomially decaying step sizes are the usual family to choose from. The exercise finds exactly which decay rates are allowed.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader applies the $p$-series test to both sums. The admissible exponents form a half-open interval.

::: {#exr-msf-robbins-monro-power}
#### Power-law step sizes

For which $p > 0$ does $\eta_k = 1/k^p$ satisfy the Robbins-Monro conditions?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sum_k k^{-p}$ diverges if and only if $p \le 1$, and $\sum_k k^{-2p}$ converges if and only if $2p > 1$. Both hold exactly when
$\frac{1}{2} < p \le 1$.
:::
::::

## Convex and Constrained Optimization {#sec-msf-convex-constrained}

Gradient methods only promise to find stationary points, and constraints are common in practice. This section introduces the
convex problems for which stationary points are global minima, and the Lagrangian that handles equality constraints.

### Convex Optimization

Convex optimization is a subfield of optimization that deals with minimizing convex functions over convex sets. A key property of
convex optimization problems is that any local minimum is also a global minimum, which makes them particularly well-suited for
efficient optimization algorithms. For more on this topic, see @deisenroth2020mml [Sec. 7.3, pp. 236-238], @shalev2014ml [Sec. 12.1.1, pp. 124-126] and @aggarwalLinearAlgebraOptimization2020 [Sec. 4.3, pp. 155-156].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-convex-set}
#### Convex Set

A set $\mathcal{C}$ is convex if for any two points $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{C}$, the line segment connecting them is
also in $\mathcal{C}$. That is, for any $\alpha \in [0, 1]$, $\alpha \mathbf{x} + (1-\alpha)\mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{C}$.
:::

::::

Balls and half-spaces are the basic convex sets from which feasible regions are built. The example checks both.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The norm properties of @def-norm make every norm ball convex. A half-space is convex because the condition defining it is
linear.

::: {#exm-msf-convex-set-ball}
#### Balls and half-spaces

If $\|\mathbf{x}\| \le 1$ and $\|\mathbf{y}\| \le 1$, the triangle inequality and homogeneity give
$\|\alpha\mathbf{x} + (1 - \alpha)\mathbf{y}\| \le \alpha\|\mathbf{x}\| + (1 - \alpha)\|\mathbf{y}\| \le 1$: the unit ball is
convex. If $\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{x} \le b$ and $\mathbf{a}^\top\mathbf{y} \le b$, then
$\mathbf{a}^\top(\alpha\mathbf{x} + (1 - \alpha)\mathbf{y}) \le b$: the half-space is convex.
:::
::::

A set with a hole is the simplest non-convex set, and intersections preserve convexity. The exercise covers both facts.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader finds a segment that leaves an annulus. The second part proves that convexity survives intersection.

::: {#exr-msf-convex-set-annulus}
#### An annulus and an intersection

(a) Show that $\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2 : 1 \le \|\mathbf{x}\| \le 2\}$ is not convex. (b) Show that the intersection of two
convex sets is convex.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $(1.5, 0)$ and $(-1.5, 0)$ lie in the set, but their midpoint $(0, 0)$ has norm $0 < 1$. (b) If $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$ lie
in both convex sets, every point $\alpha\mathbf{x} + (1 - \alpha)\mathbf{y}$ lies in each of them, hence in the intersection.
:::
::::

Convexity of a function is defined through the same segments, now compared with the graph. The definition requires the domain
itself to be convex, so that the segments make sense.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-convex-function}
#### Convex Function

A function $f$ is convex if its domain is a convex set and for any two points $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$ in its domain and any $\alpha \in [0, 1]$:

$$ f(\alpha \mathbf{x} + (1-\alpha)\mathbf{y}) \le \alpha f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-\alpha)f(\mathbf{y}) $$
:::

::::

Geometrically, this means that the line segment connecting any two points on the function's graph lies on or above the graph.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The squared loss is the basic convex function of machine learning. The example verifies the inequality for it directly.

::: {#exm-msf-convex-function-square}
#### The square function

For $f(x) = x^2$, $\alpha x^2 + (1 - \alpha)y^2 - (\alpha x + (1 - \alpha)y)^2 = \alpha(1 - \alpha)(x - y)^2 \ge 0$, so $f$ is
convex. By the triangle inequality, every norm is convex as well.
:::
::::

A single pair of points with a segment below the graph is enough to show non-convexity. The exercise asks for one such pair.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader proves convexity of the absolute value and finds a counterexample for the cube. Both are functions on $\mathbb{R}$.

::: {#exr-msf-convex-function-cube}
#### Absolute value and cube

Show that $f(x) = |x|$ is convex and that $g(x) = x^3$ is not convex on $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\alpha x + (1 - \alpha)y| \le \alpha|x| + (1 - \alpha)|y|$ by the triangle inequality. For $g$, take $x = -1$, $y = 0$,
$\alpha = \frac{1}{2}$: $g(-\frac{1}{2}) = -\frac{1}{8}$, but $\frac{1}{2}g(-1) + \frac{1}{2}g(0) = -\frac{1}{2} < -\frac{1}{8}$.
:::
::::

The key property announced at the start of this unit can now be stated and proved. It is the reason convex problems are
considered easy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-msf-convex-local-global}
#### Local Minima of Convex Functions

If $f$ is convex, then any local minimum of $f$ is also a global minimum.
:::

::::

Proof: let $\mathbf{x}^*$ be a local minimum and suppose $f(\mathbf{y}) < f(\mathbf{x}^*)$ for some $\mathbf{y}$. For
$\alpha \in (0, 1]$, the point $\mathbf{z}_\alpha = \alpha\mathbf{y} + (1 - \alpha)\mathbf{x}^*$ satisfies
$f(\mathbf{z}_\alpha) \le \alpha f(\mathbf{y}) + (1 - \alpha)f(\mathbf{x}^*) < f(\mathbf{x}^*)$. As $\alpha \to 0$,
$\mathbf{z}_\alpha$ enters every neighbourhood of $\mathbf{x}^*$, contradicting local minimality.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The statement fails without convexity, and a cubic shows how. The example contrasts it with the convex square.

::: {#exm-msf-convex-local-global-cubic}
#### A convex and a non-convex loss

$L(w) = w^2$ is convex, and its only local minimum $w = 0$ is global. $L(w) = w^3 - 3w$ has a local minimum at $w = 1$ with
$L(1) = -2$, but $L(w) \to -\infty$ as $w \to -\infty$, so the local minimum is not global; $L$ is not convex.
:::
::::

For a differentiable convex function, a zero gradient is therefore enough to certify a global minimum. The exercise applies this
to a quadratic in two variables.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader checks convexity, solves $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$, and concludes with @prp-msf-convex-local-global. No second-order test
is needed.

::: {#exr-msf-convex-stationary}
#### Certifying a global minimum

Show that $f(w_1, w_2) = (w_1 - 1)^2 + (w_2 + 2)^2$ is convex and find its global minimum.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each term is a convex square (@exm-msf-convex-function-square) of an affine function, and sums of convex functions are convex.
$\nabla f = (2(w_1 - 1), 2(w_2 + 2)) = \mathbf{0}$ at $(1, -2)$, a local minimum with $f = 0$; by convexity it is global.
:::
::::

### Applications in Machine Learning

Many machine learning problems can be formulated as convex optimization problems. For example, training a Support Vector Machine
(SVM) involves minimizing a convex loss function. The efficiency and guarantees of convex optimization make it a powerful tool in
the machine learning practitioner's toolbox [@shalev2014ml, Sec. 12.1, pp. 124-126; @deisenroth2020mml, Secs. 7.3, 12.3, pp. 236-238, 383].

### Lagrange Multipliers

Constrained optimization problems involve minimizing or maximizing a function subject to constraints on the variables. A common
method for solving such problems is the method of Lagrange multipliers.

For a problem of the form:

minimize $f(\mathbf{x})$ subject to $g(\mathbf{x}) = 0$

we introduce a new variable $\lambda$, called a Lagrange multiplier, and define the Lagrangian function:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lagrangian}
#### Lagrangian

For a constrained optimization problem with objective $f(\mathbf{x})$ and constraint $g(\mathbf{x}) = 0$, the Lagrangian is:

$$ \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \lambda g(\mathbf{x}) $$

where $\lambda$ is the Lagrange multiplier.
:::

::::

The solution to the constrained optimization problem can be found by finding the stationary points of the Lagrangian, which
involves solving the system of equations:

$$ \nabla_{\mathbf{x}, \lambda} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}, \lambda) = 0 $$

This method can be extended to handle inequality constraints as well, using the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. Constrained
optimization is used in many machine learning algorithms, such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) [@deisenroth2020mml, Secs. 7.2, 12.3.1, pp. 233-236, 383].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The point of a line closest to the origin is the simplest constrained problem. The stationarity equations of the Lagrangian solve
it in two lines.

::: {#exm-msf-lagrangian-closest-point}
#### Closest point on a line

Minimize $x^2 + y^2$ subject to $x + y - 1 = 0$. With $\mathcal{L} = x^2 + y^2 - \lambda(x + y - 1)$, stationarity gives
$2x = \lambda$, $2y = \lambda$ and $x + y = 1$, so $x = y = \frac{1}{2}$, $\lambda = 1$, and the minimum value is $\frac{1}{2}$.
:::
::::

When the constraint set is a circle, the stationarity equations have several solutions, and the objective must be compared at
each. The exercise works through such a case.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader solves the Lagrange equations for a linear objective on a circle. Two stationary points appear, the minimum and the
maximum.

::: {#exr-msf-lagrangian-circle}
#### A linear objective on a circle

Minimize $f(x, y) = x + y$ subject to $x^2 + y^2 = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $g = x^2 + y^2 - 2$, stationarity gives $1 = 2\lambda x$ and $1 = 2\lambda y$, so $x = y = 1/(2\lambda)$, and the constraint
gives $2x^2 = 2$, $x = \pm 1$. At $(1, 1)$, $f = 2$ (the maximum, $\lambda = \frac{1}{2}$); at $(-1, -1)$, $f = -2$ (the minimum,
$\lambda = -\frac{1}{2}$).
:::
::::

## Information Theory and Inference {#sec-information-theory}

Information theory provides a mathematical framework for quantifying information. This section defines entropy, the KL divergence
and mutual information, and then the two estimation principles, maximum likelihood and maximum a posteriori, that turn these
quantities into training objectives.

### Entropy

Entropy is a key concept in information theory that measures the uncertainty of a random variable. It quantifies the average
amount of information needed to specify the state of a random variable. For more on this topic, see @chambert-loirInformationTheory2022 [Secs. 1.1-1.3, pp. 23-35] and @theodoridis2025ml [Sec. 2.5, pp. 54-61].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-entropy}
#### Shannon Entropy

For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $p(x)$, the Shannon entropy is defined as:

$$ H(X) = -\sum_{i=1}^n p(x_i) \log p(x_i) $$
:::

::::

The logarithm is the natural logarithm, so the entropy is measured in nats. With $\log_2$ in place of $\log$ it is measured in
bits; the entropy in bits is the entropy in nats divided by $\log 2$. A distribution that is sharply peaked around a
few values will have a low entropy, while a distribution that is spread more evenly across many values will have a higher entropy.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A fair coin, a fair die and the spam variable of @exm-msf-bernoulli-spam span a range of uncertainty. Their entropies are
ordered accordingly.

::: {#exm-msf-entropy-coin-die}
#### Coin, die and spam

Measured in bits, with $\log_2$ in place of $\log$: a fair coin has $H = -2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1}{2} = 1$ bit
($\log 2 \approx 0.693$ nats), a fair die $H = \log_2 6 \approx 2.585$ bits, and $\operatorname{Bern}(0.3)$ has
$H = -0.3\log_2 0.3 - 0.7\log_2 0.7 \approx 0.881$ bits, less than the fair coin because it is less
uncertain.
:::
::::

The two extreme cases, no uncertainty and maximal spread, have simple entropies. The exercise computes them and one
intermediate case.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader evaluates the entropy of a constant, of a uniform variable, and of a skewed three-valued variable. The answers are
whole or half bits.

::: {#exr-msf-entropy-extremes}
#### Extreme and intermediate entropies

Compute the entropy of a constant random variable, of a uniform variable on $n$ values, and of the distribution
$(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{4}, \frac{1}{4})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A constant has $p = 1$ on one value, and $1 \cdot \log 1 = 0$, so $H = 0$. The uniform variable has
$H = -n \cdot \frac{1}{n}\log\frac{1}{n} = \log n$. In bits, the third has $H = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 2 + \frac{1}{4}\log_2 4 +
\frac{1}{4}\log_2 4 = 1.5$ bits.
:::
::::

For a continuous random variable the sum becomes an integral against the density. The result behaves differently from the discrete
entropy.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-differential-entropy}
#### Differential Entropy

For a continuous random variable with probability density function $p(x)$, the differential entropy is:

$$ H(X) = -\int p(x) \log p(x) dx $$
:::

::::

Unlike Shannon entropy, differential entropy can be negative. The Gaussian distribution has the maximum differential entropy among
all distributions with the same variance [@theodoridis2025ml, Sec. 12.8.1, pp. 620-621; @bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 2.5.4, pp. 50-51].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The uniform density on an interval has a constant integrand, so the integral is immediate. It also shows how the entropy becomes
negative.

::: {#exm-msf-differential-entropy-uniform}
#### Uniform on an interval

For $p(x) = 1/a$ on $[0, a]$, $H(X) = -\int_0^a \frac{1}{a}\log\frac{1}{a}\,dx = \log a$. For $a = \frac{1}{2}$ this is
$-\log 2 \approx -0.693$ nats, or $-1$ bit: a density concentrated on a short interval has negative differential entropy.
:::
::::

The Gaussian's entropy is the benchmark mentioned above. The exercise derives its closed form.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader takes the expectation of $-\log$ of the Gaussian density. Only the variance of $X$ is needed.

::: {#exr-msf-differential-entropy-gaussian}
#### Entropy of a Gaussian

Show that $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has $H(X) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-\log p(x) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}$. Taking expectations, with
$\mathbb{E}[(X - \mu)^2] = \sigma^2$, gives $\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi
e\sigma^2)$.
:::
::::

### Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence

The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, also known as relative entropy, is a measure of how one probability distribution diverges
from a second, expected probability distribution.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-kl-divergence}
#### Kullback-Leibler Divergence

For two discrete probability distributions $p$ and $q$, the KL divergence is
defined as:

$$ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q) = \sum_{i} p(i) \log\left(\frac{p(i)}{q(i)}\right) $$

For continuous distributions $p(x)$ and $q(x)$, it is:

$$ D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x) \log\left(\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right) dx $$
:::

::::

The KL divergence is always non-negative ($D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q) \ge 0$) and is zero if and only if $p$ and $q$ are the same
distribution. However, it is not a true distance metric because it is not symmetric, i.e., $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q) \neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \,\Vert\, p)$.
In machine learning, the KL divergence is often used as a loss function to measure the dissimilarity between a model's predicted
distribution and the true data distribution [@bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 2.5.5, pp. 51-53; @chambert-loirInformationTheory2022, Sec. 1.3, pp. 32-34].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Two Bernoulli distributions are enough to see the asymmetry. The example computes the divergence in both directions, in nats.

::: {#exm-msf-kl-bernoulli}
#### Two coins

For $p = \operatorname{Bern}(0.5)$ and $q = \operatorname{Bern}(0.3)$: $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q) = 0.5\log\frac{0.5}{0.3} + 0.5\log\frac{0.5}{0.7} \approx
0.0872$, while $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q \,\Vert\, p) = 0.3\log\frac{0.3}{0.5} + 0.7\log\frac{0.7}{0.5} \approx 0.0823$. Both are positive, and they
differ.
:::
::::

Between two Gaussians with the same variance, the KL divergence has a closed form. The exercise derives it.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader writes the log-ratio of the two densities and takes its expectation under $p$. Only the first two moments of $p$ are
needed.

::: {#exr-msf-kl-gaussians}
#### KL divergence between Gaussians

Show that $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma^2) \,\Vert\, \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma^2)) = \frac{(\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \frac{(x - \mu_2)^2 - (x - \mu_1)^2}{2\sigma^2}$. Under $p$, $\mathbb{E}[(x - \mu_1)^2] = \sigma^2$ and
$\mathbb{E}[(x - \mu_2)^2] = \sigma^2 + (\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2$, so the expectation is $\frac{(\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}$. It is
symmetric in this special case and vanishes exactly when $\mu_1 = \mu_2$.
:::
::::

### Mutual Information

Mutual information measures the mutual dependence between two random variables. It quantifies the amount of information obtained
about one random variable through observing the other random variable. The mutual information of two random variables $X$ and $Y$
is the KL divergence between their joint distribution and the product of their marginal distributions:

$$ I(X; Y) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(x,y) \,\Vert\, p(x)p(y)) = \sum_{x,y} p(x,y) \log\left(\frac{p(x,y)}{p(x)p(y)}\right) $$

It can also be expressed in terms of entropy:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-mutual-information}
#### Mutual Information

The mutual information between random variables $X$ and $Y$:

$$ I(X; Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) $$
:::

::::

where $H(X|Y)$ is the conditional entropy of $X$ given $Y$. This shows that the mutual information is the reduction in uncertainty
about one variable given knowledge of the other. Mutual information is always non-negative and is zero if and only if the two
variables are independent [@theodoridis2025ml, Sec. 2.5, pp. 56-61; @bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 2.5.7, p. 54; @chambert-loirInformationTheory2022, Sec. 1.3, p. 35].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When one variable determines the other, all the uncertainty of the second is removed. On the die, the face determines the parity.

::: {#exm-msf-mutual-information-parity}
#### Face and parity

In bits, $H(Y) = \log_2 2 = 1$ bit, and $H(Y|X) = 0$ because $Y$ is a function of $X$. So $I(X; Y) = 1 - 0 = 1$ bit: the face tells everything about
the parity.
:::
::::

Partial dependence gives a mutual information strictly between zero and the entropies. The exercise computes it for the two
indicators of the die.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader uses the KL form of the mutual information with the table of @exr-msf-joint-pmf-yz. The answer is small but positive.

::: {#exr-msf-mutual-information-yz}
#### Parity and low face

Compute $I(Y; Z)$ in bits for the die, and state $I(U; V)$ for the two independent coins of @exr-msf-independence-coins.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both marginals are uniform, so $p_Y(y)p_Z(z) = \frac{1}{4}$. Then $I(Y; Z) = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{6}\log_2\frac{1/6}{1/4} + 2 \cdot
\frac{1}{3}\log_2\frac{1/3}{1/4} = \frac{1}{3}\log_2\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\log_2\frac{4}{3} \approx -0.195 + 0.277 = 0.082$
bits. For independent coins every log-ratio is $\log_2 1 = 0$, so $I(U; V) = 0$.
:::
::::

### Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) is a method for estimating the parameters of a statistical model. Given a set of i.i.d.
(independent and identically distributed) data points $S = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ drawn from a distribution $p(x|\theta)$
parameterized by $\theta$, the likelihood function is the probability of observing the data as a function of the parameters:

$$ p(S | \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i | \theta) $$

The principle of Maximum Likelihood Estimation is to choose the parameters $\theta$ that maximize the likelihood function. This is
equivalent to finding the parameters that make the observed data most probable.

In practice, it is often easier to work with the log-likelihood function, since the logarithm converts the product into a sum and
does not change the location of the maximum.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-maximum-likelihood}
#### Maximum Likelihood Estimate

The Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) of $\theta$ is therefore given by:

$$ \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \arg\max_{\theta} \log p(S | \theta) = \arg\max_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^n \log p(x_i | \theta) $$
:::

::::

MLE is a cornerstone of statistical inference and is widely used to train machine learning models [@shalev2014ml, Sec. 24.1, pp. 295-296; @bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 2.3.2, pp. 37-38; @aggarwalProbabilityStatisticsMachine2024, Sec. 6.2, p. 246].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For coin tosses the maximum likelihood estimate is the observed frequency of heads. The example derives this from the
log-likelihood.

::: {#exm-msf-mle-bernoulli}
#### Estimating a coin's bias

With $k$ heads in $n$ independent $\operatorname{Bern}(p)$ tosses, the log-likelihood is $k\log p + (n - k)\log(1 - p)$. Setting the derivative
$k/p - (n - k)/(1 - p)$ to zero gives $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = k/n$; for $7$ heads in $10$ tosses, $\hat{p} = 0.7$.
:::
::::

For Gaussian data with known variance, maximising the likelihood is the same as minimising squared error. The exercise derives the
resulting estimate of the mean.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader writes the Gaussian log-likelihood, drops the constant terms, and differentiates. The estimate is the sample mean.

::: {#exr-msf-mle-gaussian-mean}
#### The mean of a Gaussian

Find $\hat{\mu}_{\mathrm{MLE}}$ for i.i.d. data from $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with $\sigma^2$ known, and evaluate it on $(2, 4, 9)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\log p(S | \mu) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (x_i - \mu)^2$. Its derivative
$\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_i (x_i - \mu)$ vanishes at $\hat{\mu} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i$, which is a maximum since $\log p(S | \mu)$ is a
downward parabola. For $(2, 4, 9)$, $\hat{\mu} = 5$.
:::
::::

### Maximum A Posteriori Estimation

Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation is a Bayesian alternative to MLE that incorporates prior knowledge about the parameters.
Using Bayes' theorem, the posterior distribution of the parameters given the data is:

$$ p(\theta | S) = \frac{p(S | \theta) p(\theta)}{p(S)} $$

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-msf-map-estimation}
#### Maximum A Posteriori Estimate

The MAP estimate is the mode of the posterior distribution:

$$ \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\theta} p(\theta | S) = \arg\max_{\theta} p(S | \theta) p(\theta) $$
:::

::::

Since the denominator $p(S)$ does not depend on $\theta$, it can be ignored in the optimization. Taking logarithms, we get:

$$ \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\theta} [\log p(S | \theta) + \log p(\theta)] $$

The MAP estimate reduces to the MLE when the prior $p(\theta)$ is uniform (i.e., when we have no prior preference for any
particular parameter value). The prior allows us to incorporate domain knowledge or regularization into the estimation process.
For example, a Gaussian prior on the parameters corresponds to $\ell_2$ regularization, while a Laplace prior corresponds to
$\ell_1$ regularization [@bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 2.6.2, pp. 56-57; @deisenroth2020mml, Secs. 8.3.2, 9.5, pp. 269, 316; @aggarwalProbabilityStatisticsMachine2024, Sec. 7.7, pp. 331-332].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A Beta prior on a coin's bias acts like a few imaginary tosses added to the data. The example compares the MAP estimate with the
MLE of @exm-msf-mle-bernoulli.

::: {#exm-msf-map-beta}
#### A coin with a Beta prior

With a prior density proportional to $p^{a - 1}(1 - p)^{b - 1}$ and $k$ heads in $n$ tosses, the log-posterior is
$(k + a - 1)\log p + (n - k + b - 1)\log(1 - p)$ up to a constant, maximised at $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \frac{k + a - 1}{n + a + b - 2}$.
For $a = b = 2$ and $7$ heads in $10$ tosses, $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{MAP}} = 8/12 = 2/3$, pulled from $0.7$ toward $\frac{1}{2}$.
:::
::::

The correspondence between Gaussian priors and $\ell_2$ regularization can be derived in one line for a linear model. The exercise
asks for the derivation and the resulting estimate.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader writes the negative log-posterior of a one-parameter regression with a Gaussian prior. It is a penalised least squares
objective.

::: {#exr-msf-map-ridge}
#### Gaussian prior and ridge regression

Let $y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(wx_i, \sigma^2)$ independently and $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$. Show that $\hat{w}_{\mathrm{MAP}}$ minimises
$\sum_i (y_i - wx_i)^2 + \lambda w^2$ with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2$, and find it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Up to constants, $-\log p(S | w) - \log p(w) = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (y_i - wx_i)^2 + \frac{w^2}{2\tau^2}$; multiplying by
$2\sigma^2$ gives the stated objective. Setting its derivative $-2\sum_i x_i(y_i - wx_i) + 2\lambda w$ to zero gives
$\hat{w}_{\mathrm{MAP}} = \frac{\sum_i x_iy_i}{\sum_i x_i^2 + \lambda}$, which shrinks the least squares estimate toward $0$.
:::
::::

## Cross-Entropy and Entropy Regularization {#sec-msf-cross-entropy}

Two information-theoretic quantities appear directly in training objectives. Cross-entropy is the standard classification loss,
and policy entropy is the bonus that encourages exploration in reinforcement learning.

### Cross-Entropy

Cross-entropy is a measure from information theory that quantifies the difference between two probability distributions. It is
widely used as a loss function in classification tasks. For two discrete probability distributions $p$ and $q$, the cross-entropy
is defined as:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cross-entropy-discrete}
#### Cross-Entropy (Discrete)

$$ H(p, q) = -\sum_{i} p(i) \log q(i) $$
:::

::::

Cross-entropy is the average surprise, measured with $q$, of outcomes that actually follow $p$. The example evaluates it for a
one-hot target.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When $p$ is one-hot, only one term of the sum survives. This is the situation of a labelled training example.

::: {#exm-msf-cross-entropy-one-hot}
#### A one-hot target

For $p = (1, 0)$ and a prediction $q = (0.8, 0.2)$, $H(p, q) = -\log 0.8 \approx 0.223$ nats.
:::
::::

With a non-degenerate $p$, every outcome contributes. The exercise computes such a cross-entropy in bits.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader evaluates the formula for a fair coin predicted by a biased model. The answer exceeds the entropy of the fair coin.

::: {#exr-msf-cross-entropy-bits}
#### A fair coin, a biased model

Compute $H(p, q)$ in bits for $p = (\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})$ and $q = (\frac{1}{4}, \frac{3}{4})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$H(p, q) = -\frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{3}{4} = 1 + \frac{1}{2}\log_2\frac{4}{3} \approx 1.208$ bits,
more than $H(p) = 1$ bit.
:::
::::

For continuous distributions:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cross-entropy-continuous}
#### Cross-Entropy (Continuous)

$$ H(p, q) = -\int p(x) \log q(x) dx $$
:::

::::

The continuous version replaces the sum by an integral, just as differential entropy does. When $q = p$ it reduces to the
differential entropy, measured in nats.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The standard Gaussian against itself gives the differential entropy of @exr-msf-differential-entropy-gaussian, in nats. This is
the smallest cross-entropy any $q$ can achieve for this $p$.

::: {#exm-msf-cross-entropy-gaussian-self}
#### A Gaussian against itself

For $p = q = \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $H(p, q) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e) \approx 1.419$ nats.
:::
::::

Shifting the model's mean away from the data's mean raises the cross-entropy. The exercise computes by how much.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader takes the expectation of $-\log q$ under $p$ for two Gaussians with equal variance. The excess over the entropy matches
@exr-msf-kl-gaussians.

::: {#exr-msf-cross-entropy-gaussians}
#### Two Gaussians

Compute $H(p, q)$ in nats for $p = \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma^2)$ and $q = \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma^2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-\log q(x) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \frac{(x - \mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}$, and under $p$,
$\mathbb{E}[(x - \mu_2)^2] = \sigma^2 + (\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2$. So $H(p, q) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma^2) + \frac{(\mu_1 -
\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2}$: the entropy of $p$ plus the KL divergence.
:::
::::

The two exercises above both found the entropy of $p$ plus an excess equal to the KL divergence. The cross-entropy can be
decomposed as [@bishop2024deeplearning, Sec. 2.5.5, eq. 2.100]:

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-msf-cross-entropy-decomposition}
#### Cross-Entropy Decomposition

$$ H(p, q) = H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q) $$
:::

::::

where $H(p)$ is the entropy of $p$ and $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q)$ is the KL divergence from $p$ to $q$. Proof: $-\sum_i p(i)\log q(i) =
-\sum_i p(i)\log p(i) + \sum_i p(i)\log\frac{p(i)}{q(i)}$, which is $H(p) + D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q)$ (all three in nats, or all
three in bits with $\log_2$ throughout). Since $H(p)$ is constant with
respect to $q$, minimizing the cross-entropy is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two coins of @exm-msf-kl-bernoulli make the decomposition concrete. All three quantities are computed in nats.

::: {#exm-msf-cross-entropy-decomposition-coins}
#### Two coins again

For $p = \operatorname{Bern}(0.5)$, $q = \operatorname{Bern}(0.3)$: $H(p) = \log 2 \approx 0.6931$, $H(p, q) = -0.5\log 0.3 - 0.5\log 0.7 \approx
0.7803$, and their difference $0.0872$ is $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q)$.
:::
::::

For a one-hot target the entropy term vanishes, so the cross-entropy loss is itself a KL divergence. The exercise makes this
explicit for one training example.

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The reader evaluates the binary cross-entropy loss below on one prediction. The decomposition then explains why it equals a KL
divergence.

::: {#exr-msf-cross-entropy-one-hot-kl}
#### One-hot targets

For a label $y = 1$ and a prediction $\hat{y} = 0.9$, compute the binary cross-entropy loss, and show that for one-hot $p$,
$H(p, q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\ell(0.9, 1) = -\log 0.9 \approx 0.105$ nats. A one-hot $p$ has $H(p) = -1 \cdot \log 1 = 0$, so by @prp-msf-cross-entropy-decomposition
$H(p, q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \,\Vert\, q)$.
:::
::::
